title: The 1956 Dartmouth workshop
text:
CHAPTER 8. TURING 1950 AND THE BIRTH OF AI
SECTION 8.2. THE 1956 DARTMOUTH WORKSHOP

Artificial intelligence as a named research field began with a funding proposal. In the late summer of 1955 four researchers asked the Rockefeller Foundation to support a summer study at Dartmouth College "on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it." The proposal coined the term "artificial intelligence." The workshop itself, held in the summer of 1956, produced no single breakthrough, but it brought together the people who would lead AI for the next two decades and set the field's agenda and optimism. This section looks at the proposal, the people, what happened, and what it led to.

1. The organizers

  John McCarthy (1927-2011), then a young assistant professor of mathematics at Dartmouth College, was the driving force. He had worked on automata theory and had co-edited, with Claude Shannon, a volume called "Automata Studies" (published 1956), whose contributions he felt had mostly ignored the question of intelligent behavior. He chose the name "artificial intelligence" partly to give the new field a clear identity separate from automata theory and from cybernetics (Section 7.1).

  Marvin Minsky (1927-2016), then a Junior Fellow at Harvard, had built the SNARC neural learning machine in 1951 (Section 7.3) and written a PhD thesis on neural networks.

  Nathaniel Rochester (1919-2001) of IBM was the chief architect of the IBM 701, IBM's first commercial scientific computer, and had simulated neural networks on IBM machines (Section 7.3).

  Claude Shannon (1916-2001) of Bell Labs, the founder of information theory and of switching theory (Section 2.1), had written on chess-playing computers (Section 8.3).

In early 1955 McCarthy approached the Rockefeller Foundation about funding a summer seminar for about ten participants; in June he and Shannon met with Robert Morison, the foundation's director of biological and medical research. The formal proposal, "A Proposal for the Dartmouth Summer Research Project on Artificial Intelligence," is dated August 31, 1955, and was submitted in early September 1955. The foundation provided a smaller grant than requested (commonly reported as $7,500).

2. The proposal

The proposal is short and remarkably confident. Its opening states:

    "We propose that a 2 month, 10 man study of artificial intelligence be carried out during the summer of 1956 at Dartmouth College in Hanover, New Hampshire. The study is to proceed on the basis of the conjecture that every aspect of learning or any other feature of intelligence can in principle be so precisely described that a machine can be made to simulate it."

And it continues that "a significant advance can be made in one or more of these problems if a carefully selected group of scientists work on it together for a summer."

It listed seven aspects of "the artificial intelligence problem":

  1. Automatic computers: if a machine can do a job, an automatic calculator can be programmed to simulate it; the limitation is not the speed or memory of computers but our inability to write programs that use what we have.
  2. How can a computer be programmed to use a language: speculating that much of human thought consists of manipulating words according to rules of reasoning and rules of conjecture.
  3. Neuron nets: how a set of (hypothetical) neurons can be arranged to form concepts.
  4. Theory of the size of a calculation: measuring the efficiency of computations, avoiding exhaustive search.
  5. Self-improvement: a truly intelligent machine would carry out activities best described as self-improvement.
  6. Abstractions: classifying types of abstraction and describing how machines can form them from sensory and other data.
  7. Randomness and creativity: the difference between creative thinking and unimaginative competent thinking might lie in the injection of some randomness, guided by intuition.

Each organizer also described his own research plans. Shannon proposed applying information theory concepts to computing machines and brain models; Minsky proposed a machine that would learn to behave intelligently in an environment using abstract models; Rochester proposed studying originality in machine performance; McCarthy proposed studying the relation of language to intelligence and constructing an artificial language that a computer could use for reasoning.

Read this list as an engineer and compare it with this book's remaining chapters. Natural language (Chapters 17-19), neural networks (Chapters 10, 13, 16), computational complexity and heuristic search (Section 9.3), self-improvement and learning, abstraction and representation learning, and randomness in search (Monte Carlo methods, stochastic gradient descent): almost every theme of the next 70 years appears in the proposal. The organizers' estimate of how long it would take was wildly optimistic; their list of problems was not.

3. The workshop

The workshop is usually said to have lasted about six to eight weeks in the summer of 1956, beginning around June 18. It was not a conference with a fixed program but an informal gathering in which participants came and went, held discussions and worked on their own projects. Not all invited participants attended for the whole time, and over the summer more than ten others came for shorter periods. Ray Solomonoff stayed for the whole period and kept notes, which survive, as do notes by Trenchard More, who replaced Rochester for three weeks.

Participants and visitors included, besides the organizers (Rochester only partly):

  - Ray Solomonoff, who later founded algorithmic probability and the theory of inductive inference (a mathematical theory of prediction based on the shortest programs that generate data, related to Kolmogorov complexity).
  - Oliver Selfridge, of MIT Lincoln Laboratory, working on pattern recognition (he would publish "Pandemonium" in 1959; Section 7.3).
  - Trenchard More, then a Princeton graduate student.
  - Arthur Samuel of IBM, who was developing a checkers program that learned (Section 8.3).
  - Allen Newell and Herbert Simon of the RAND Corporation and Carnegie Institute of Technology, who brought the most concrete result.

Samuel later recalled it as "very interesting, very stimulating, very exciting." But the participants did not produce a joint program of work; several, notably Newell and Simon, were already deep in their own projects.

4. The Logic Theorist

The one working AI program on display, in the sense of a program that did something people regarded as requiring intelligence, was the Logic Theorist by Allen Newell, Herbert Simon and Cliff Shaw. It proved theorems from Chapter 2 of Whitehead and Russell's Principia Mathematica (Section 1.2), searching for proofs using heuristics: rules of thumb that guided the search toward promising steps instead of trying everything. Section 9.1 describes it in detail.

Newell and Simon had developed it in 1955-1956 and first ran it on the JOHNNIAC computer at RAND. Simon is often quoted as having told his students in January 1956 that over the Christmas holiday he and Newell had "invented a thinking machine"; treat the wording as a recollection. At Dartmouth the other participants were reportedly less impressed than Newell and Simon expected, perhaps because the program had already been developed outside the group. But it was a concrete demonstration that a computer could carry out a task, logical proof, that was considered a hallmark of human intelligence.

5. The two traditions at Dartmouth

The Dartmouth proposal included both "neuron nets" and language-based reasoning, and the participants represented both the learning tradition (Minsky's earlier work, Rochester's simulations, Selfridge, Solomonoff, Samuel) and the symbolic tradition (Newell and Simon, McCarthy's language for reasoning). In the years that followed, mainstream AI moved strongly toward the symbolic side:

  - Newell and Simon developed the General Problem Solver (1957-1959) and a theory of human problem solving as symbol manipulation (Section 9.1), and later formulated the "physical symbol system hypothesis" (1976): that a physical symbol system has the necessary and sufficient means for general intelligent action.
  - McCarthy invented LISP (1958; Section 9.2) and proposed the "Advice Taker" (1959), a system that would reason with formal logic from common-sense knowledge.
  - Minsky moved away from neural networks toward symbolic representations, frames and the "society of mind."

Meanwhile neural network learning continued largely outside the Dartmouth group, most notably with Frank Rosenblatt's perceptron (1957-1958; Section 10.1).

6. The labs that followed

Within a few years the Dartmouth participants had founded the institutions that dominated AI for decades:

  - MIT: McCarthy and Minsky started the MIT Artificial Intelligence Project in 1958-1959, which became part of Project MAC (1963) and later the MIT AI Laboratory.
  - Carnegie Tech (later Carnegie Mellon University): Newell and Simon built a center of AI and cognitive psychology research.
  - Stanford: McCarthy moved to Stanford in 1962 and founded the Stanford Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (SAIL).
  - IBM: Samuel's checkers work and Rochester's projects continued there, though IBM became cautious about publicizing "thinking machines."

In Britain, AI research developed in parallel, for example at Edinburgh under Donald Michie (Section 3.3) from the 1960s.

Funding came substantially from the US Department of Defense's Advanced Research Projects Agency (ARPA, later DARPA), founded in 1958, whose Information Processing Techniques Office, led first by J. C. R. Licklider from 1962, funded AI, time-sharing and networking research generously and with few strings attached in the 1960s.

7. Optimism and its costs

The founders were very optimistic. In 1957-1958 Simon and Newell predicted that within ten years a digital computer would be world chess champion, would discover and prove an important new mathematical theorem, and would write music of considerable aesthetic value, among other predictions. Simon wrote in 1965 that "machines will be capable, within twenty years, of doing any work a man can do," and Minsky made similarly bold statements in the 1960s. (These quotations appear in many histories, though exact phrasings vary between sources.) A computer did not become chess champion until 1997 (IBM's Deep Blue defeating Garry Kasparov), forty years later.

Why the optimism? Early programs made fast progress on problems that were hard for humans but well defined (logic proofs, algebra word problems, games), and the founders underestimated problems that are easy for humans but hard to formalize (perception, common sense, natural language, movement). This pattern, later called Moravec's paradox (after roboticist Hans Moravec, who described it in the 1980s with others), is familiar to anyone who has tried to make a robot pick up an unfamiliar object. When the predictions failed, the disappointment contributed to funding cuts and the "AI winters" (Chapter 11).

8. The 2006 and later anniversaries

In 2006 Dartmouth hosted a 50th anniversary conference, "AI@50," attended by several original participants, including McCarthy, Minsky, Selfridge, More and Solomonoff. By then AI had passed through two winters, and statistical machine learning was flourishing. Twenty years later, the field's capabilities and the debates about them had changed again, driven by deep learning and large language models.

9. Assessment

Was the Dartmouth workshop the birth of AI? In a narrow sense it produced little research. In a broader sense it:

  - gave the field its name and an explicit, ambitious research program;
  - established the conjecture that every aspect of intelligence can be precisely described and simulated, the field's founding hypothesis;
  - created a social network of founders who built the major labs;
  - framed a list of problems that remains recognizably current.

10. Summary

  - The proposal by McCarthy, Minsky, Rochester and Shannon (dated August 31, 1955) coined "artificial intelligence" and conjectured that every aspect of intelligence can be described precisely enough for a machine to simulate it.
  - It listed seven problems: automatic computers, language, neuron nets, size of calculations, self-improvement, abstractions, randomness and creativity.
  - The workshop ran for roughly six to eight weeks in summer 1956 at Dartmouth; participants included Solomonoff, Selfridge, More, Samuel, Newell and Simon.
  - Newell, Simon and Shaw's Logic Theorist was the main working program presented.
  - The founders went on to establish AI labs at MIT, Carnegie Tech and Stanford, largely funded by ARPA; their optimistic predictions proved premature, setting the stage for later disillusionment.
